summary: Second Gauge checks India's weekly reservoir storage figures against NISAR radar and flags the ones worth checking again: 9 weekly figures, at reservoirs radar usually tracks well, sit more than two standard deviations from what the radar water area suggests. For every bulletin reservoir we could locate, it measures the reservoir's water area on each NISAR pass from June to November 2026 and compares it with the live storage the Central Water Commission reports for 178 reservoirs each week. We tuned the water mapping on half of the reservoirs and scored it once on the other half: on those 40 held-out reservoirs, radar water area tracks the reported storage closely (Pearson r > 0.7) at 15, and very closely (r > 0.9) at 7. The app shows every reservoir, including the ones where radar and the bulletin disagree, and answers the challenge's polarization question with a count: HH follows the bulletin better than HV at 59 of 80 reservoirs. Reservoirs fill during the monsoon, when clouds hide them from optical satellites; NISAR's L-band radar sees them anyway, every 12 days, for free.
details:
What it does. Pick a reservoir on the map or in the table. Second Gauge draws the water NISAR saw on each pass, plots radar water area against the bulletin's live storage over the season, gives the agreement (r) for HH and for HV, and marks passes that disagree with the season's fit as "look again". A separate "Look again" list gathers those passes from reservoirs radar usually tracks well (r ≥ 0.7): 9 passes from June to November 2026. A disagreement can come from either source; the list says where a second look is worth it.

How it works.

1. For each reservoir, find NISAR L2 GCOV passes (June to November 2026) in the Alaska Satellite Facility catalogue and keep one orbit track and one observation mode.

2. Read only the 80 m HH and HV grids around the reservoir with HTTP range requests, about 15 MB per pass instead of a 2 GB file.

3. Map water: an automatic HH threshold (Otsu's method) set on the reservoir and 4 km of shore, pooled over the season; passes whose land brightness jumps are dropped; only water connected to the reservoir's permanent pool and inside its Global Dam Watch outline counts. The threshold never sees the bulletin.

4. Match each pass to bulletin storage on the same date and compute r per reservoir.

To keep the bulletin an independent check, the reservoirs were split by a hash of their names before any tuning. Water-mapping variants were compared on the tuning half only; the chosen method was then scored once on the 40 held-out reservoirs.

What we found. 129 of the 171 bulletin names were matched to a reservoir outline; 80 had at least 8 radar passes on a bulletin week. On the 40 held-out reservoirs, r > 0.7 at 15 and r > 0.9 at 7 (median r 0.59). HH beats HV at 59 of 80: calm water reflects the radar pulse away from the satellite and goes dark in HH while the land around it stays bright; in HV, water and dry ground both return little. Radar area tracks storage poorly where reservoirs are steep sided (area changes little as they fill), where smooth dry shore looks as dark as water at 80 m, and where one bad pass upsets a season. Those reservoirs stay on the map with their low r.

Why it matters. Storage figures decide irrigation releases, drinking-water planning and drought declarations. A free, independent check that works through monsoon cloud tells a reader which official figures the radar agrees with and which deserve a second look.

Tools. Python (h5py, NumPy, SciPy, pyproj, Pillow), Leaflet, Playwright for end-to-end tests, Vercel for hosting.

Use of AI tools. AI tools (large language models) were used to brainstorm and choose the idea, research data sources, write and debug code, and draft text. All results come from running the code on real NISAR and CWC data, checked by automated tests. The three background paintings on the site (the reservoir in the monsoon, the gauge post and the aerial view) were made with an AI image model and each carries a visible "AI-generated image" watermark. No NASA logos, flags or mission markings appear in them. Every map, chart, number and radar water outline comes from the real data, not from AI. The demo video's voiceover was made with an AI voice tool from a clone of a team member's voice; the video says so on screen and in its file metadata, and its map frames are captures of the live app.
